claim: The intestinal epithelium undergoes complete turnover in approximately 3 days.
source: This rapid turnover protects against insults from bacterial toxins and metabolites, dietary antigens, mutagens, and exposure to DNA damaging agents including irradiation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Leblond and Walker, 1956

claim: Intestinal stem cells (ISCs) reside at the bottom of crypt and generate the precursors for the specialized differentiated cells.
source: The processes of normal tissue turnover and intestinal regeneration are driven by intestinal stem cells (ISCs) that reside at the bottom of crypt and generate the precursors for the specialized differentiated cells (Barker, 2014; Li and Clevers, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barker, 2014 and Li and Clevers, 2010

claim: The ISC compartment includes two functionally and molecularly distinct stem cell populations.
source: It has been extensively reported that ISC compartment includes two functionally and molecularly distinct stem cell populations (Barker, 2014; Li and Clevers, 2010; Gehart and Clevers, 2015): The active crypt base columnar (CBC) stem cells (Sato et al., 2011), (Barker et al., 2007) and a more dormant, reserve ISC population that reside above the crypt base and exhibit no Wnt pathway activity, also referred as +4 cells due to their position at the crypt (Montgomery et al., 2011; Sangiorgi and Capecchi, 2008; Tian et al., 2011; Takeda et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: CBCs are identified and isolated based on the expression of Lgr5, a Wnt target gene.
source: The CBCs often identified and isolated based on the expression of Lgr5, a Wnt target gene (Barker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barker et al., 2007

claim: High canonical Wnt activity promotes CBC self-renewal and proliferation during homeostasis.
source: During homeostasis, steady-state proliferation of CBCs is driven by extrinsic niche signals – high canonical Wnt activity promotes CBC self-renewal and proliferation (Barker et al., 2007; Miyoshi, 2017) while BMP signals antagonize it (Kosinski et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barker et al., 2007; Miyoshi, 2017; and Kosinski et al., 2007

claim: BMP signals antagonize CBC self-renewal and proliferation.
source: During homeostasis, steady-state proliferation of CBCs is driven by extrinsic niche signals – high canonical Wnt activity promotes CBC self-renewal and proliferation (Barker et al., 2007; Miyoshi, 2017) while BMP signals antagonize it (Kosinski et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kosinski et al., 2007

claim: Reserve ISCs represent a slow-cycling population of stem cells that are resistant to high doses of ionizing radiation.
source: In contrast to the active CBCs, the reserve ISCs represent a slow-cycling population of stem cells that are resistant to high doses of ionizing radiation and appear dispensable for homeostasis (Sangiorgi and Capecchi, 2008; Yousefi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sangiorgi and Capecchi, 2008 and Yousefi et al., 2016

claim: Reserve ISCs are identified through CreERT knockin reporter alleles at the Bmi1 and Hopx loci, as well as by an Tert-CreERT transgene.
source: These reserve ISCs are identified through CreERT knockin reporter alleles at the Bmi1 and Hopx loci, as well as by an Tert-CreERT transgene (Montgomery et al., 2011; Sangiorgi and Capecchi, 2008; Tian et al., 2011; Takeda et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Reserve ISCs do not have an active Wnt signaling pathway and are refractory to Wnt signals in their resting state.
source: Reserve ISCs do not have an active Wnt signaling pathway and are refractory to Wnt signals in their resting state (Takeda et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takeda et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014; and Li et al., 2016

claim: During epithelial regeneration upon stresses, reserve ISCs give rise to Wnthigh Lgr5+ CBCs.
source: During epithelial regeneration upon stresses, reserve ISCs give rise to Wnthigh Lgr5+ CBCs that generate the precursor cells of the specialized differentiated cells (Tian et al., 2011; Takeda et al., 2011; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tian et al., 2011; Takeda et al., 2011; and Li et al., 2014

claim: Lgr5-CreERT- or Bmi1-CreERT-marked cells can act as the cells of origin of intestinal cancer in mice.
source: In addition, it has been documented that Lgr5-CreERT- or Bmi1-CreERT-marked cells can act as the cells of origin of intestinal cancer in mice (Sangiorgi and Capecchi, 2008; Barker et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sangiorgi and Capecchi, 2008 and Barker et al., 2009

claim: MicroRNAs play important roles in stress-activated pathways.
source: Mounting evidence indicates that microRNAs play important roles in stress-activated pathways (Leung and Sharp, 2010; Mendell and Olson, 2012; Emde and Hornstein, 2014) and in control of somatic stem cell fate and tumorigenesis (Gangaraju and Lin, 2009; Sun and Lai, 2013; Yi and Fuchs, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Leung and Sharp, 2010; Mendell and Olson, 2012; and Emde and Hornstein, 2014

claim: MicroRNAs play important roles in control of somatic stem cell fate and tumorigenesis.
source: Mounting evidence indicates that microRNAs play important roles in stress-activated pathways (Leung and Sharp, 2010; Mendell and Olson, 2012; Emde and Hornstein, 2014) and in control of somatic stem cell fate and tumorigenesis (Gangaraju and Lin, 2009; Sun and Lai, 2013; Yi and Fuchs, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gangaraju and Lin, 2009; Sun and Lai, 2013; and Yi and Fuchs, 2011

claim: Global ablation of microRNA activity through genetic deletion of Dicer demonstrated that microRNAs are critical for homeostasis of intestinal epithelium.
source: Global ablation of microRNA activity through genetic deletion of the microRNA processing enzyme Dicer demonstrated that microRNAs are critical for homeostasis of intestinal epithelium (McKenna et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to McKenna et al., 2010

claim: miR-143/145 are essential for intestinal epithelial regeneration after injury, acting non cell-autonomously in sub-epithelial myofibroblasts.
source: Particularly, miR-143/145 are essential for intestinal epithelial regeneration after injury, acting non cell-autonomously in sub-epithelial myofibroblasts (Chivukula et al., 2014), indicating potential importance of microRNA activity in intestinal regeneration.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chivukula et al., 2014

claim: miR-31 becomes overexpressed in colorectal cancer.
source: In the ISC compartment, the function of miR-31 is of a particular interest, as it becomes overexpressed in colorectal cancer (Bandrés et al., 2006; Cottonham et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2013) and increases during the progression of inflammation-associated intestinal neoplasia (Olaru et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bandrés et al., 2006; Cottonham et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; and Yang et al., 2013

claim: miR-31 increases during the progression of inflammation-associated intestinal neoplasia.
source: In the ISC compartment, the function of miR-31 is of a particular interest, as it becomes overexpressed in colorectal cancer (Bandrés et al., 2006; Cottonham et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2013) and increases during the progression of inflammation-associated intestinal neoplasia (Olaru et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olaru et al., 2011

claim: miR-31 is enriched in mammary stem/progenitor cells.
source: In addition, it has been reported that miR-31 is enriched in mammary stem/progenitor cells, suggesting a potential role in somatic stem cells (Ibarra et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ibarra et al., 2007

claim: MiR-31 expression levels are the highest in the Lgr5-GFPhigh crypt base columnar stem cells.
source: MiR-31 expression levels are the highest in the Lgr5-GFPhighcrypt base columnar stem cells, intermediate in Lgr5-GFPlow transit-amplifying cell population and the lowest in Lgr5-GFPneg populations (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Higher level of miR-31 was found in Hopx+ reserve ISCs than that in bulk epithelial cells.
source: Higher level of miR-31 was also found in Hopx+ reserve ISCs than that in bulk epithelial cells (Figure 1A), based on isolation with Hopx-CreERT;mTmG alleles from mice 15 hr after tamoxifen injection.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A

claim: miR-31 is predominantly expressed in the epithelial cells of intestinal crypt, including stem cells and transit amplifying cells.
source: Consistently, in situ hybridization revealed that miR-31 expression levels are generally higher in the crypts than villi. MiR-31 is predominantly expressed in the epithelial cells of intestinal crypt, including stem cells and transit amplifying cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B

claim: MiR-31 levels transiently and markedly drop by 24 hours post-γ-IR.
source: MiR-31 levels transiently and markedly drop by 24 hours (coincident with full proliferative arrest/DNA damage response), and then sharply upregulated 48 hours post-γ-IR (during initiation of regenerative proliferation from the radioresistant ISCs), and then return to baseline levels within one week (after full recovery) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C

claim: MiR-31 is sharply upregulated 48 hours post-γ-IR during initiation of regenerative proliferation from the radioresistant ISCs.
source: MiR-31 levels transiently and markedly drop by 24 hours (coincident with full proliferative arrest/DNA damage response), and then sharply upregulated 48 hours post-γ-IR (during initiation of regenerative proliferation from the radioresistant ISCs), and then return to baseline levels within one week (after full recovery) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C

claim: miR-31 expressing cells are located in the regenerative foci known to exhibit high Lgr5 expression and Wnt pathway activity.
source: In situ hybridization reveals miR-31 expressing cells to be located in the regenerative foci known to exhibit high Lgr5 expression and Wnt pathway activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Dox administration in TRE-miR31 mice resulted in a significant reduction in body weight after 2 weeks.
source: MiR-31 induction in response to Dox administration in TRE-miR31 mice resulted in a significant reduction in body weight after 2 weeks (Figure 1E) and intestinal lengths were moderately, but significantly shorter than controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Intestinal lengths were moderately, but significantly shorter in TRE-miR31 mice than controls after 2 weeks of Dox treatment.
source: MiR-31 induction in response to Dox administration in TRE-miR31 mice resulted in a significant reduction in body weight after 2 weeks (Figure 1E) and intestinal lengths were moderately, but significantly shorter than controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Dox treatment of TRE-miR31 mice for 2 weeks resulted in expansion of intestinal crypts.
source: Dox treatment of TRE-miR31 mice for 2 weeks resulted in expansion of intestinal crypts (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by histologic images and quantification shown in Figure 1F

claim: More mitotic cells were found in the TRE-miR31 crypts.
source: More mitotic cells were found in the TRE-miR31 crypts (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), while more apoptotic cells were detected at the top of TRE-miR31 villi (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B

claim: More apoptotic cells were detected at the top of TRE-miR31 villi.
source: More mitotic cells were found in the TRE-miR31 crypts (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), while more apoptotic cells were detected at the top of TRE-miR31 villi (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B

claim: The number of Lgr5+ ISCs increased in TRE-miR31 mice after 10 day Dox treatment.
source: The number of Lgr5+ ISCs increased in TRE-miR31 mice after 10 day Dox treatment, while no significant difference was found between them after 7 days of Dox induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and FACS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D

claim: There were fewer differentiated cells including enteroendocrine, goblet and Paneth cells in TRE-miR31 intestine than the controls.
source: In addition, there were fewer differentiated cells including enteroendocrine, goblet and Paneth cells in TRE-miR31 intestine than the controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B), indicating an impaired cell differentiation.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B

claim: Loss of miR-31 led to a significant reduction in crypt height with fewer proliferative cells.
source: Despite this, loss of miR-31 led to a significant reduction in crypt height with fewer proliferative cells (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by histologic images and quantification shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D

claim: Loss of miR-31 gave rise to a certain number of apoptotic cells throughout the crypt-villus axis.
source: Interestingly, loss of miR-31 gave rise to a certain number of apoptotic cells throughout the crypt-villus axis, while apoptotic cells are predominantly presented at the tip of control villi and very rare apoptotic cells are presented in crypt-villus axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5C,D

claim: Deletion of miR-31 led to increased numbers of enteroendocrine and Paneth cells.
source: Deletion of miR-31 also led to increased numbers of enteroendocrine and Paneth cells, while the number of goblet cells remained unaltered in miR-31 KO intestines (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A,B

claim: The phenotype of shortened crypts with fewer proliferative cells was found in cKO intestine.
source: Moreover, the phenotype of shortened crypts with fewer proliferative cells was also found in cKO intestine (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by histologic images and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A,B

claim: Loss of miR-31 gave rise to more apoptotic cells in cKO intestinal epithelium, including in cKO crypts.
source: Loss of miR-31 gave rise to more apoptotic cells in cKO intestinal epithelium, including in cKO crypts, while cleaved-caspase3+ apoptotic cells were nearly entirely absent from control crypts (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C,D

claim: Upward movement of BrdU+ cells from crypts to villi was enhanced in TRE-miR31 mice.
source: We further analyzed DNA synthesis and migration of epithelial cells along the crypt-villus axis after a single pulse of BrdU. Upward movement of BrdU+ cells from crypts to villi was enhanced in TRE-miR31 mice, and this movement was impaired in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claim: Upward movement of BrdU+ cells from crypts to villi was impaired in miR-31−/− mice.
source: We further analyzed DNA synthesis and migration of epithelial cells along the crypt-villus axis after a single pulse of BrdU. Upward movement of BrdU+ cells from crypts to villi was enhanced in TRE-miR31 mice, and this movement was impaired in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claim: Lgr5+ ISC frequency was markedly increased in TRE-miR31 intestine.
source: Lgr5+ ISC frequency was markedly increased in TRE-miR31, and significantly reduced in miR-31−/− and cKO intestine (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Lgr5+ ISC frequency was significantly reduced in miR-31−/− and cKO intestine.
source: Lgr5+ ISC frequency was markedly increased in TRE-miR31, and significantly reduced in miR-31−/− and cKO intestine (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FACS data shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The frequency of actively proliferating Lgr5-GFP+/EdU+ cells is higher in TRE-miR31 mice.
source: A 1.5 hr pulse of EdU incorporation demonstrated that the frequency of actively proliferating Lgr5-GFP+/EdU+ cells is higher in TRE-miR31 mice and conversely lower in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The frequency of actively proliferating Lgr5-GFP+/EdU+ cells is lower in miR-31−/− mice.
source: A 1.5 hr pulse of EdU incorporation demonstrated that the frequency of actively proliferating Lgr5-GFP+/EdU+ cells is higher in TRE-miR31 mice and conversely lower in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2D

claim: miR-31 induction increased the frequency of budding organoids in vitro.
source: In line with these in vivo findings, miR-31 induction increased the frequency of budding organoids in vitro, and caused more buds per organoid and more elongated crypts (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by organoid culture data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: miR-31 induction in the intestine increases the height of traced lineages derived from Lgr5-CreERT-marked ISCs.
source: Furthermore, lineage-tracing assay reveals that miR-31 induction in the intestine increases the height of traced lineages derived from Lgr5-CreERT-marked ISCs (Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2F,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: miR-31 induction significantly repressed Hopx expression.
source: Interestingly, miR-31 induction significantly repressed Hopx expression, while deletion of miR-31 increased it (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Deletion of miR-31 increased Hopx expression.
source: Interestingly, miR-31 induction significantly repressed Hopx expression, while deletion of miR-31 increased it (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2H

claim: miR-31 induction in the intestine repressed lineage tracing from Hopx-CreERT-marked reserve ISCs.
source: Consistently, miR-31 induction in the intestine repressed lineage tracing from Hopx-CreERT-marked reserve ISCs (Figure 2I, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2I, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: Deletion of miR-31 within intestinal epithelium induced quiescence (residence in G0) in Lgr5-GFP+ cells concomitant to an increase in apoptosis and a decrease in cycling (G1/S/G2/M).
source: In contrast to miR-31 overexpression, deletion of miR-31 within intestinal epithelium induced quiescence (residence in G0) in Lgr5-GFP+ cells concomitant to an increase in apoptosis and a decrease in cycling (G1/S/G2/M) (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Higher frequency of apoptotic organoids and compromised budding was found in the cKO crypts.
source: In agreement, higher frequency of apoptotic organoids and compromised budding was found in the cKO crypts (Figure 2K), and more apoptotic cells were found inside of the cKO organoids (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by organoid culture data shown in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: There were significantly fewer regenerative foci and fewer proliferative cells per regenerative focus in cKO mice 4 days post-γ-IR.
source: However, by 4 days post-γ-IR, there were significantly fewer regenerative foci and fewer proliferative cells per regenerative focus in cKO mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by histology and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Intestinal regeneration in response to γ-IR was significantly impaired in miR-31−/− mice.
source: Consistently, intestinal regeneration in response to γ-IR was significantly impaired in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by histology and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: In the intestine of TRE-miR31 mice pre-treated for 2 weeks with Dox, there were more regenerative foci with higher numbers of proliferative cells than in the control mice.
source: Conversely, in the intestine of TRE-miR31 mice pre-treated for 2 weeks with Dox, there were more regenerative foci with higher numbers of proliferative cells than in the control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by histology and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Loss of miR-31 increased apoptosis in the crypts 2 and 4 hours post-irradiation prior to any overt histological changes.
source: To understand the phenotype resulting from miR-31 modulation, we assayed for apoptotic cells in cKO mice at early stages after irradiation. Loss of miR-31 increased apoptosis in the crypts 2 and 4 hours post-irradiation prior to any overt histological changes (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Apoptotic events occur with the highest frequently in CBC cells in cKO crypts compared to control mice.
source: Quantification of apoptotic cell position analysis reveals that apoptotic events occur with the highest frequently in CBC cells, but are still found in transit-amplifying and +4 zones of cKO crypts, compared to control mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Flow cytometry confirmed higher frequency of late apoptotic Lgr5+ cells (AnnexinV+/7AAD+) and lower frequency of early apoptotic Lgr5+ cells (AnnexinV+/7AAD−) and live Lgr5+ cells (AnnexinV-/7AAD-) in cKO mice, relative to controls.
source: Further, flow cytometry for live cell and apoptotic markers within the Lgr5-GFP+ population confirmed higher frequency of late apoptotic Lgr5+ cells (AnnexinV+/7AAD+) and lower frequency of early apoptotic Lgr5+ cells (AnnexinV+/7AAD−) and live Lgr5+ cells (AnnexinV-/7AAD-) in cKO mice, relative to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: More Lgr5-GFP+ cells resided in G0 relative to G1/S/G2/M in cKO mice 2 hours after γ-IR.
source: Next, we examined its effect on cell proliferation. Cell cycle analysis indicates that more Lgr5-GFP+ cells resided in G0 relative to G1/S/G2/M in cKO mice 2 hours after γ-IR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: Expression levels of Lgr5 were dramatically up-regulated in TRE-miR31 mice and prominently down-regulated in miR-31−/− mice at multiple time points after irradiation.
source: In agreement, expression levels of Lgr5 were dramatically up-regulated in TRE-miR31 mice and prominently down-regulated in miR-31−/− mice at multiple time points after irradiation (Figure 3C), and consequently miR-31 induction promoted lineage regeneration from Lgr5+ cells in response to irradiation (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C

claim: miR-31 induction promoted lineage regeneration from Lgr5+ cells in response to irradiation.
source: In agreement, expression levels of Lgr5 were dramatically up-regulated in TRE-miR31 mice and prominently down-regulated in miR-31−/− mice at multiple time points after irradiation (Figure 3C), and consequently miR-31 induction promoted lineage regeneration from Lgr5+ cells in response to irradiation (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3D,E

claim: miR-31 induction promoted epithelial regeneration from the Hopx+ reserve stem cells.
source: Lineage-tracing assay revealed that miR-31 induction promoted epithelial regeneration from the Hopx+ reserve stem cells (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: The number and the size of regenerative foci originating from Hopx-CreER;Rosa26-LoxP-Stop-LoxP-LacZ-marked cells were markedly reduced in miR-31−/− mice.
source: Conversely, the number and the size of regenerative foci originating from Hopx-CreER;Rosa26-LoxP-Stop-LoxP-LacZ-marked cells were markedly reduced in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3G

claim: The frequency of LacZ+/Ki67+ cells was significantly lower in miR-31−/− mutants compared to controls.
source: In line with this, the frequency of LacZ+/Ki67+ cells was significantly lower in miR-31−/− mutants compared to controls (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Wnt pathway activity was strikingly absent from CBCs of miR-31−/− crypts, appearing only faintly above the crypt base in the early TA zones.
source: In contrast, Wnt pathway activity was strikingly absent from CBCs of miR-31−/− crypts, appearing only faintly above the crypt base in the early TA zones (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by Axin2-LacZ reporter data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Wnt activity was expanded in TRE-miR31 crypts.
source: Conversely, Wnt activity was expanded in TRE-miR31 crypts (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by Axin2-LacZ reporter data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The number of nuclear β-Catenin-positive cells was significantly reduced in miR-31−/− intestinal crypts at 2 and 4 months of age.
source: In agreement, the number of nuclear β-Catenin-positive cells was significantly reduced in miR-31−/− intestinal crypts at 2 and 4 months of age (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: The number of nuclear β-Catenin-positive cells increase in TRE-miR31 crypts 14 days and 2 months after Dox induction.
source: Conversely, they increase in TRE-miR31 crypts 14 days and 2 months after Dox induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Expression levels of Ctnnb1 (encoding β-Catenin) and the Wnt targets, Ccnd1 (encoding Cyclin D1), Myc and Axin2 were significantly reduced in miR-31−/− intestine both at the RNA and protein levels.
source: Consistently, the expression levels of Ctnnb1 (encoding β-Catenin) and the Wnt targets, Ccnd1 (encoding Cyclin D1), Myc and Axin2 were significantly reduced in miR-31−/− intestine both at the RNA and protein levels (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: Expression levels of Ctnnb1, Ccnd1, Myc and Axin2 were enhanced in TRE-miR31 intestinal epithelium following 2 weeks of Dox induction.
source: In contrast, expression levels of the above genes were enhanced in TRE-miR31 intestinal epithelium following 2 weeks of Dox induction (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: The reduction in Ctnnb1 and Wnt targets was confirmed in conditional miR-31 KO intestine.
source: The reduction in Ctnnb1 and Wnt targets was further confirmed in conditional miR-31 KO intestine (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Ccnd1, Ctnnb1, Myc and Axin2 were markedly increased in miR-31 over-expressing HCT116 cells, relative to controls.
source: Ccnd1, Ctnnb1, Myc and Axin2 were markedly increased in miR-31 over-expressing cells, relative to controls (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in HCT116 cells shown in Figure 4H

claim: Ccnd1, Ctnnb1, Myc and Axin2 were downregulated upon miR-31 inhibition in HCT116 cells.
source: Conversely, these genes were downregulated upon miR-31 inhibition (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in HCT116 cells shown in Figure 4H

claim: β-Catenin was up-regulated in the presence of miR-31 mimics, and down-regulated upon miR-31 inhibition in HCT116 cells.
source: Consistently, β-Catenin was up-regulated in the presence of miR-31 mimics, and down-regulated upon miR-31 inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data in HCT116 cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: miR-31 induction enhanced Wnt activity in HCT116 cells, while inhibition of miR-31 repressed it.
source: The Wnt reporter (Topflash/Fopflash) assay using HCT116 cells further confirmed that miR-31 induction enhanced Wnt activity, while inhibition of miR-31 repressed it (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4I

claim: miR-31 induction via TRE-miR31 was sufficient to maintain crypt organoid growth and budding in the absence of R-spondin.
source: Interestingly, we observed that miR-31 induction via TRE-miR31 was sufficient to maintain crypt organoid growth and budding in the absence of R-spondin (Figure 4J,K) and that the Dox-treated TRE-miR31 organoids can be normally passaged at least five times, similar to the organoids cultured with R-spondin (Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by organoid culture data shown in Figure 4J,K,L

claim: BMP-specific Smad1/5/8 and TGFβ-specific Smad2/3 phosphorylation were significantly increased in miR-31−/− intestine.
source: BMP-specific Smad1/5/8 and TGFβ-specific Smad2/3 phosphorylation were significantly increased in miR-31−/− intestine (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and downregulated in TRE-miR31 intestine (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting an inhibitory effect of miR-31 on BMP and TGFβ signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: BMP-specific Smad1/5/8 and TGFβ-specific Smad2/3 phosphorylation were downregulated in TRE-miR31 intestine.
source: BMP-specific Smad1/5/8 and TGFβ-specific Smad2/3 phosphorylation were significantly increased in miR-31−/− intestine (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and downregulated in TRE-miR31 intestine (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting an inhibitory effect of miR-31 on BMP and TGFβ signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: There was a significant increase on the expression of BMP target genes including Id1, Id2, Id3, Msx1, Msx2 and Junb and TGFβ target genes Cdkn1c (p57), Cdkn1a (p21), Cdkn2a (p16), and Cdkn2b (p15) in miR-31−/− intestine.
source: Consistently, we observed a significant increase on the expression of BMP target genes including Id1, Id2, Id3, Msx1, Msx2 and Junb and TGFβ target genes Cdkn1c (p57), Cdkn1a (p21), Cdkn2a (p16), and Cdkn2b (p15) in miR-31−/− intestine (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B

claim: BMP and TGFβ targets were repressed upon forced expression of miR-31 in TRE-miR31 intestine following 2 weeks of Dox induction.
source: Conversely, BMP and TGFβ targets were repressed upon forced expression of miR-31 in TRE-miR31 intestine following 2 weeks of Dox induction (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The upregulation of BMP and TGFβ targets was confirmed upon conditional miR-31 deletion in cKO intestine.
source: The upregulation of BMP and TGFβ targets was further confirmed upon conditional miR-31 deletion in cKO intestine (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D,E

claim: BMP-specific Smad1/5/8 and TGFβ-specific Smad2/3 phosphorylation were increased in miR-31 cKO cultured organoids.
source: BMP-specific Smad1/5/8 and TGFβ-specific Smad2/3 phosphorylation were also increased in miR-31 cKO cultured organoids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Down-regulation of p-Smad2/3 and p-Smad1/5/8 was found in HCT116 cells treated with miR-31 mimics.
source: In line with the in vivo findings, we found down-regulation of p-Smad2/3 and p-Smad1/5/8 in HCT116 cells treated with miR-31 mimics, and their up-regulation in cells treated with miR-31 inhibitor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data in HCT116 cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Up-regulation of p-Smad2/3 and p-Smad1/5/8 was found in HCT116 cells treated with miR-31 inhibitor.
source: In line with the in vivo findings, we found down-regulation of p-Smad2/3 and p-Smad1/5/8 in HCT116 cells treated with miR-31 mimics, and their up-regulation in cells treated with miR-31 inhibitor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting data in HCT116 cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: Inhibition of miR-31 resulted in significant increases in BMP- and TGFβ-responsive luciferase activities, and miR-31 mimics decreased them.
source: Luciferase assays using BMP- and TGFβ-responsive luciferase reporters, BRE-Luc and CAGA-Luc, respectively, revealed that inhibition of miR-31 resulted in significant increases in luciferase activities, and that miR-31 mimics decreased them (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5F,G

claim: Increasing concentrations of the BMP inhibitor Noggin in organoid culture was able to rescue the budding defect in miR-31 cKO organoids in a dose-dependent manner.
source: More importantly, increasing concentrations of the BMP inhibitor Noggin in organoid culture was able to rescue the budding defect in miR-31 cKO organoids in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5H,I).
evidence: Supported by organoid culture data shown in Figure 5H,I

claim: The expression of Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Smad3, Smad4, Bmpr1a and Tgfbr2 was significantly upregulated in miR-31−/− intestine.
source: The expression of Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Smad3, Smad4, Bmpr1a and Tgfbr2 was significantly upregulated in miR-31−/− intestine (Figure 6A) and remarkably downregulated in TRE-miR31 intestine following Dox induction (Figure 6B), suggesting that they are negatively regulated by miR-31.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The expression of Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Smad3, Smad4, Bmpr1a and Tgfbr2 was remarkably downregulated in TRE-miR31 intestine following Dox induction.
source: The expression of Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Smad3, Smad4, Bmpr1a and Tgfbr2 was significantly upregulated in miR-31−/− intestine (Figure 6A) and remarkably downregulated in TRE-miR31 intestine following Dox induction (Figure 6B), suggesting that they are negatively regulated by miR-31.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The upregulation of Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Smad3, Smad4, and Bmpr1a was confirmed in conditional miR-31 KO intestine.
source: The upregulation of these putative target genes was further confirmed in conditional miR-31 KO intestine (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Bmpr1a and Smad4 protein levels were validated in miR-31 mutant mice.
source: Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Bmpr1a and Smad4 were selected for further validation at protein level (Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C) and in organoids cultured from miR-31 cKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by Western blotting and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A

claim: Mutation of the miR-31 3'UTR binding site in luciferase constructs for Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Bmpr1a, Smad3 and Smad4 abrogated repression by miR-31.
source: Next, we validated the direct repression of target transcripts by miR-31 activity using WT-3'UTR-luciferase constructs for Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Bmpr1a, Smad3 and Smad4. Mutation of the miR-31 3'UTR binding site in these constructs abrogated this repression (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: CLIP-PCR assays confirmed that transcripts of Axin1, Dkk1, Gsk3b, Smad3, Smad4 and Bmpr1a were highly enriched in Ago2 immunoprecipitates, and that increasing miR-31 activity augmented their enrichment.
source: Furthermore, RNA crosslinking, immunoprecipitation, and RT-PCR (CLIP-PCR) assays with Ago2 antibodies confirmed that transcripts of Axin1, Dkk1, Gsk3b, Smad3, Smad4 and Bmpr1a were highly enriched in Ago2 immunoprecipitates, and that increasing miR-31 activity augmented their enrichment (Figure 6G), providing evidence that miR-31 directly binds to these transcripts.
evidence: Supported by CLIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Derepression of Axin1, Gsk3b, Dkk1, Smad3, Bmpr1a, Smad4 and Tgfbr2 was observed in miR-31−/− intestine after irradiation.
source: Next, we asked whether these targets functionally contribute to impaired regeneration in miR-31−/− mice. Derepression of these target transcripts was observed in miR-31−/− intestine after irradiation (Figure 6H,I).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6H,I

claim: Wnt activity was reduced, while the BMP and TGFβ activities were increased in miR-31−/− intestine after irradiation.
source: As a consequence, Wnt activity was reduced, while the BMP and TGFβ activities were increased in miR-31−/− intestine, evidenced by β-Catenin, p-Smad1/5/8 and p-Smad2/3 immunohistochemistry assays (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6J

claim: miR-31 mimics promoted proliferation of HCT116, SW480 and LOVO colon cancer cells in vitro.
source: We tested the role of miR-31 in intestinal tumorigenesis and observed that miR-31 mimics promoted proliferation of HCT116, SW480 and LOVO colon cancer cells in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by MTT proliferation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Inhibition of miR-31 with anti-miR-31 abrogated growth of HCT116, SW480 and LOVO colon cancer cells.
source: Conversely, inhibition of miR-31 with anti-miR-31 abrogated growth of these cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by MTT proliferation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Tumor volume and weight were increased in miR-31 mimic-treated tumors, and markedly reduced in miR-31 knockdown tumors in xenograft assays.
source: We further performed xenograft assays using miR-31 mimics- and inhibitor-treated HCT116 cells. Thirty days after grafting, tumor volume and weight were increased in miR-31 mimic-treated tumors, and markedly reduced in miR-31 knockdown tumors (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 7A

claim: The decrease in tumor size from miR-31 inhibition coincided with the reduction in Ki67+ and Cyclin D1+ proliferating cells.
source: The decrease in tumor size from miR-31 inhibition coincided with the reduction in Ki67+ and Cyclin D1+ proliferating cells (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), and correlated with reduced Wnt activity and increased BMP and TGFβ activities (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: There was a marked decrease in both tumor size and number in miR-31−/− mice in the AOM-DSS model.
source: To verify these findings in more physiologically relevant settings, we examined tumor formation in the AOM-DSS (Azoxymethane-Dextran Sodium Sulfate) model of the inflammation-driven colorectal adenocarcinoma (De Robertis et al., 2011). In comparison with the controls, we observed a marked decrease in both tumor size and number in miR-31−/− mice (Figure 7C), along with a concomitant reduction in proliferating cells (Figure 7D,E), and reduced Wnt pathway and increased BMP and TGFβ activity (Figure 7D,F).
evidence: Supported by AOM-DSS model data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Loss of miR-31 in Vil-Cre;Apcflox/+ mice remarkably reduced tumor burden.
source: This tumor-promoting effect of miR-31 in mice became even more evident when miR-31 was deleted in Vil-Cre;Apcflox/+ mice. Intestinal adenomas form in this mouse model upon loss of heterozygosity at the Apc locus, which is relevant to human disease in that spontaneous loss of Apc is found in the vast majority of human colorectal cancer (Kinzler et al., 1991; Nagase et al., 1992). Loss of miR-31 in this animal model remarkably reduced tumor burden (Figure 7G), which was associated with decreased Wnt activity, enhanced BMP and TGFβ signaling, and decreased proliferating cells (Figure 7H–J and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data from Vil-Cre;Apcflox/+ mice shown in Figure 7G

claim: The miR-31 targets Axin1, Dkk1, Gsk3β, Smad4 and Bmpr1a were up-regulated in the miR-31 null tumors.
source: Correspondingly, the miR-31 targets Axin1, Dkk1, Gsk3β, Smad4 and Bmpr1a were up-regulated in the miR-31 null tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: The STAT3 and NF-κB signaling pathways were activated in response to γ-IR.
source: Interestingly, the STAT3 and NF-κB signaling pathways were shown to be activated in response to γ-IR, evidenced by p-STAT3 and p65 levels, respectively (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 8B,C

claim: The activation of the STAT3 pathway occurred mainly in the regenerative foci where miR-31 is highly induced.
source: The activation of the STAT3 pathway occurred mainly in the regenerative foci where miR-31 is highly induced, while NF-κB was more prominently activated in villi where little miR-31 is present and not in the regenerative foci (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 8D

claim: miR-31 expression was significantly induced upon IL-6 treatment in mICc12 intestinal epithelial cells.
source: To verify whether active STAT3 signaling could induce miR-31 expression, mICc12 intestinal epithelial cells were treated with IL-6, a known activator of the STAT3 signaling. Indeed, miR-31 expression was significantly induced upon IL-6 treatment (Figure 8E), concomitant with the activation of the STAT3 pathway (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 8E,F

claim: Inhibition of STAT3 signaling with Stattic prominently dampened miR-31 induction response to IL-6 treatment.
source: In contrast, inhibition of STAT3 signaling with Stattic prominently dampened miR-31 induction response to IL-6 treatment (Figure 8G), and reduced STAT3 signaling (Figure 8H).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 8G,H

claim: This inhibitory effect on miR-31 expression was validated using Stat3 siRNA.
source: This inhibitory effect on miR-31 expression was further validated using Stat3 siRNA (Figure 8I,J).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 8I,J

claim: miR-31 was induced by IL-6 in the organoid cultures.
source: Importantly, miR-31 was induced by IL-6 in the organoid cultures, indicating that this is an epithelial cell-autonomous mechanism (Figure 8K).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in organoids shown in Figure 8K

claim: IL-6 is able to induce luciferase activity of miR-31 promoter, while mutation of the p-STAT3 binding site blocked it.
source: Luciferase reporter assays reveal that IL-6 is able to induce its activity, while mutation of the p-STAT3 binding site blocked it (Figure 8L).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 8L

claim: Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays show that p-STAT3 is recruited to its binding site on the miR-31 promoter.
source: Furthermore, Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays show that p-STAT3 is recruited to its binding site on the miR-31 promoter (Figure 8M).
evidence: Supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 8M

claim: miR-31 drives ISC proliferation during homeostasis and regeneration in response to ionizing radiation injury.
source: Here we show that miR-31 drives ISC proliferation, and protects ISCs against apoptosis, both during homeostasis and regeneration in response to ionizing radiation injury.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data throughout the manuscript

source: Here we show that miR-31 drives ISC proliferation, and protects ISCs against apoptosis, both during homeostasis and regeneration in response to ionizing radiation injury.
